hero.intro: Notice friction in familiar situations before choosing a solution. Record what you saw, separate your interpretation, and create a three-entry Problem Discovery Journal.

questions.prompt: Which statement is an observation if you directly saw it?
options: Two visitors asked staff which queue to join
The venue must build a digital platform
questions.explanation: A specific event you saw is an observation; broad demand claims and proposed solutions are assumptions.

questions.prompt: What should you do when delay or frequency is unknown?
options: Label it unknown and plan how to check
questions.explanation: Keep uncertainty visible; neither invented measurements nor zero are justified without evidence.

questions.prompt: What does a planned journal entry represent?
options: An investigation plan, not collected evidence
Proof that the problem occurs frequently
questions.explanation: Planned entries can guide observation but must not be represented as research already completed.

scenes.title: Notice friction
scenes.visual: Adult visitor pauses at a venue entrance with several unbranded signs; documentary realism in Dubai.
scenes.narration: Problems often appear as small moments of friction: waiting, repeating a task, searching for information, or finding a workaround. Today, practise noticing those moments. You are not choosing a product yet. You are collecting clues about what people experience.

scenes.title: Describe what happened
scenes.visual: Observer writes notes without filming people; editable fact-versus-interpretation cards added in post.
scenes.narration: Write what happened in a specific situation. “Two visitors asked where to check in” is an observation if you saw it. “Everyone needs a new app” is an assumption. Keep the observation separate from what you think it means. A small clue does not prove a market.

scenes.title: Look at existing workarounds
scenes.visual: Visitor asks a staff member, checks a paper map, and follows a direction; no identifiable documents.
scenes.narration: People may already cope by asking someone, using a spreadsheet, making a note, or avoiding the task. Record that workaround. Ask what it helps with and what may still be difficult. Do not assume your preferred solution would be better before understanding what works today.

scenes.title: Keep uncertainty visible
scenes.visual: Editable source labels: observed firsthand, reported by someone, planned not yet observed.
scenes.narration: Record the source of each entry. Did you observe it yourself, hear about it, or only plan to investigate? If you do not know the impact or frequency, say so. Do not turn a guess into a number. Planned observation is useful preparation, but it is not collected evidence.

scenes.title: Explore respectfully
scenes.visual: Observer watches a general venue process, notebook closed while walking; no covert camera or personal details.
scenes.narration: Choose a familiar setting where observation is appropriate. Avoid recording names, faces or private details. Ask permission before interviewing or recording someone, and follow the setting’s access rules. Focus on the process and the situation, not on judging the people involved.

blocks.prompt:
Create a beginner-friendly educational explainer for LYNQ Venture Studio Academy, Module 1.2 Lesson 06: “See Problems in Everyday Life.” Desired final edit about 150 seconds, 16:9, 1080p. Combine realistic documentary-style process moments, editable observation-versus-assumption diagrams, and a genuine worksheet screen recording. Palette navy #0B2338, teal #087D79, mint #BCF2DF and white. Contemporary Dubai public/venue setting, diverse adult cast, calm curious English narrator, no exaggerated frustration or success imagery.

Teaching objectives: notice everyday friction before selecting a solution; record specific observations and existing workarounds; distinguish observation, interpretation and next question; label firsthand/reported/planned sources; keep unknown impact/frequency explicit; and observe respectfully. Use FICTIONAL adult event visitors looking for check-in directions. Label example graphics “Illustrative example.” Never imply a real LYNQ client case, validated demand, measured market size or collected research. No invented interview quotes, confidential details, names or identifiable contact data.

Use these six scenes and exact narration in sequence. Target around 25 seconds per final scene, adjusting after narrator read-through with natural diagram holds. Record one consistent voice track separately. Generate short footage only in durations supported by the selected Gemini/Veo model/account. An eight-second shot plan is optional where supported. Assemble clips, editable diagrams, narration and captions in a video editor; do not claim one prompt generates a complete polished film.

SCENE 1 — Notice friction. Visual: Adult visitor pauses at a venue entrance with several unbranded signs; documentary realism in Dubai. Narration: “Problems often appear as small moments of friction: waiting, repeating a task, searching for information, or finding a workaround. Today, practise noticing those moments. You are not choosing a product yet. You are collecting clues about what people experience.”

SCENE 2 — Describe what happened. Visual: Observer writes notes without filming people; editable fact-versus-interpretation cards added in post. Narration: “Write what happened in a specific situation. “Two visitors asked where to check in” is an observation if you saw it. “Everyone needs a new app” is an assumption. Keep the observation separate from what you think it means. A small clue does not prove a market.”

SCENE 3 — Look at existing workarounds. Visual: Visitor asks a staff member, checks a paper map, and follows a direction; no identifiable documents. Narration: “People may already cope by asking someone, using a spreadsheet, making a note, or avoiding the task. Record that workaround. Ask what it helps with and what may still be difficult. Do not assume your preferred solution would be better before understanding what works today.”

SCENE 4 — Keep uncertainty visible. Visual: Editable source labels: observed firsthand, reported by someone, planned not yet observed. Narration: “Record the source of each entry. Did you observe it yourself, hear about it, or only plan to investigate? If you do not know the impact or frequency, say so. Do not turn a guess into a number. Planned observation is useful preparation, but it is not collected evidence.”

SCENE 5 — Explore respectfully. Visual: Observer watches a general venue process, notebook closed while walking; no covert camera or personal details. Narration: “Choose a familiar setting where observation is appropriate. Avoid recording names, faces or private details. Ask permission before interviewing or recording someone, and follow the setting’s access rules. Focus on the process and the situation, not on judging the people involved.”

SCENE 6 — Create the discovery journal. Visual: Actual Lesson 06 journal screen recording with fictional clearly labeled sample data. Narration: “Now create three journal entries. For each, note the source, context, people involved, what happened, the workaround, possible impact, interpretation, and next question. Look for a pattern without claiming proof. If you have not observed yet, label the entry as planned and choose a small observation to do next.”

Return the scene plan, timing and individual visual-shot prompts first. Generated footage must have no text, logos, captions, watermark, speaking presenters or fabricated UI. Exact LYNQ wordmark, process diagrams, source tags and subtitles are editable post-production elements. Suggested overlays: What happened / What I think / What I still need to ask; Existing workaround; Firsthand / Reported / Planned; Unknown ≠ Zero; Three-entry journal. Keep the same approved observer reference actor and wardrobe; realistic gestures and hands. Do not show covert filming or recording of private details.

Scene 6 must use actual approved Lesson 06 screen recording with fictional labeled entries. Show that a planned entry stays planned and is not treated as evidence. Never generate the product UI. End card in post: “Notice one moment. Record it honestly. Ask the next question.”

Human-produced deliverables: H.264 1920×1080 MP4, editable project/diagrams, narrator audio, thumbnail, timed English VTT/SRT and transcript, generation/reference rights provenance. Separate native-reviewed Arabic narration/captions and RTL graphics; do not auto-mirror English UI. Review mobile legibility, pacing, audio intelligibility, source/uncertainty wording, privacy and brand before publishing. No video is generated by this prototype.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Look for friction before you look for an app.

children: A problem is a difficulty someone experiences in a specific situation. It may show up as wasted time, repeated effort, confusion, missed information, extra cost, or a workaround. Your task today is to notice and record clues, not to decide that every inconvenience deserves a business.
Use a familiar setting: an event, shop, workplace process, journey, or everyday task. Choose a situation you can observe appropriately. You can explore without a business idea.
By the end, you can
Describe a moment of friction with a specific context.
Separate what happened from what you think it means.
Record an existing workaround and unknown impact.
Label whether an entry is firsthand, reported, or planned.
Create three entries and a next observation question.
Observation
What you directly saw or heard, with a clear source and context. “At check-in, two visitors asked staff which queue to join.”
Use this only if it actually happened; this example is fictional.
Interpretation
What you think it might mean. “The queue signs may not be clear.” That is a possible explanation, not a confirmed cause.
Workaround
How people manage today. “They asked a staff member.” That may work well; understand it before proposing a replacement.
Next question
What would help you check the interpretation? “Which directions did they see, and what was unclear?”
Where to look
Waiting:
where does a process slow down, and why might that be?
Repeating:
what information or action gets repeated?
Searching:
what do people struggle to find?
Workarounds:
where do notes, messages, spreadsheets or extra staff bridge a gap?
Avoiding:
what task do people skip, and what do you still need to ask?
A simple illustrative journal entry
Source:
fictional example, not learner evidence.
Context:
venue entrance before an event.
People:
first-time adult visitors.
What happened:
two visitors asked staff which queue to join.
Workaround:
staff gave directions.
Impact:
an extra step; delay and frequency are unknown.
Interpretation:
directions may be unclear; there may be another explanation.
Next question:
which signs did visitors notice?

blocks.prompt: Which statement describes what happened rather than a solution or broad claim?

options.label: Everyone wants an event app
options.feedback: That is a broad assumption or proposed solution. Start with a specific observed event, label its source, and keep interpretation separate.

options.label: Two visitors asked staff which queue to join
options.feedback: Correct for this fictional example: a specific event can be an observation if you saw it. Its cause, frequency and business value still need checking.

options.label: The venue needs a digital platform
options.feedback: That is a broad assumption or proposed solution. Start with a specific observed event, label its source, and keep interpretation separate.

children: Optional practice; this fictional example is not research evidence.
Keep the source and uncertainty visible
Observed firsthand:
you directly noticed the situation.
Reported by someone:
someone described an experience; identify the role/source without private details.
Planned — not yet observed:
something you intend to investigate. Write a plan, not a pretend result.

If impact, frequency or current alternatives are unknown, say “unknown” or “to check.” One entry cannot prove that a problem is common or worth solving commercially. You will explore affected people and problem priority in later lessons.
Observe respectfully.
Follow access rules; do not record names, faces or private details. Ask permission before interviews or recording. A general process note is enough for this journal.
Notice patterns without forcing a conclusion

After three entries, compare them. Do they share a setting, repeated step or type of friction? Write a tentative pattern and a next question. “No pattern yet” is acceptable. Choose further observation rather than inventing certainty.

Create three entries. Use firsthand observations or clearly labeled reports where you have them. If you have not observed yet, choose “Planned — not yet observed” and write an honest investigation plan.
Arabic entries use automatic text direction. Use role labels and avoid sensitive personal information. No entry is automatically treated as verified evidence.

Try four scripted guidance modes. The preview reads your current worksheet locally; it does not send information anywhere.

replies.teach: Notice friction in a specific context. Keep what happened separate from interpretation. Record existing workarounds and unknown impact. Firsthand, reported and planned entries are different sources; none automatically proves demand.
replies.guide: Create three entries. Select a truthful source/status for each. Write context, people as roles, the observation or plan, workaround, impact/unknowns, interpretation and next question. Compare entries without forcing a pattern.
replies.review:
Problem Discovery Journal check: {missing} required fields still empty. All three entries and the pattern field are present. Check source labels, unknowns, and whether interpretations are separate from facts.
This scripted check counts fields only. It cannot verify that observations happened or prove impact, frequency or demand.
replies.challenge: Could there be another explanation? Is the current workaround sufficient? Which entries are only planned? What would contradict the pattern you suspect? Avoid turning a solution preference into a problem claim.
